country.evidence_source:
[page/0/Text/10] The late 1970s witnessed a massive trend toward migration in China, with millions of migrant workers moving from rural to urban areas for better jobs and living conditions. The 2010 population census reported 261 million migrants, which was an increase of 81.03% from the previous census a decade prior (National Bureau of Statistics of China
[page/1/Text/1] 2011). In recent years, an increasing number of migrant parents have brought their children when relocating to host cities. For example, in 2015, 173,000 (33.72%) migrant children above school-age migrated to Beijing with their parents for more than 6 months (Zhao and Wei 2017). This migration allows migrant children a better education and living conditions. However, it also introduces some difculties. Due to the restriction of the Household Registration System (i.e., Hukou), rural-to-urban migrant families are still regarded as rural residents who are temporarily residing in a host city. In China, Hukou is a particular administrative-geographical unit that is assigned at birth and always classifed as rural or urban.

[page/1/Text/1] Migrant schools in China specifcally enroll rural-to-urban migrant children in grades 1–9. Some investigations have determined that 112 migrant schools were located in Beijing in 2016 and that nearly half of them were self-built primary schools without licenses (Eduthought 2018). The same situation also was found in terms of welfare: a reduced number of health care and social services exist for migrant children (Zhang et al. 2010). In addition to the limited resources and services, migrant children and adolescents often experience serious adversities in their environment, including a lower family socioeconomic status, acculturation stress, negative parenting, and discrimination by both local peers and institutions (Liu and Wang 2015).
[page/1/Text/2] Early adolescents aged 10–14 years are experiencing puberty and health changes (Arnett 2013; WHO 2001). Due to interactions between developmental changes at both the individual and social environment level, this period is crucial for subsequent individual development and achievements (Eccles et al. 1993). Large-scale studies in China have found that those migrant adversities lead to more emotional problems, poorer social and school functioning (Cheung 2013; Lin et al. 2011; Wang and Mesman 2015), and reduced well-being (Cheng et al. 2014; Ni et al. 2016) among rural-to-urban migrant adolescents and children.
